## Problem E6: Batch Cooling in a Jacketed Vessel {.unnumbered}

A batch of process liquid is held in a well-stirred, jacketed vessel. At the end of a reaction step the batch is at 90 $^\circ$C and must be cooled to 30 $^\circ$C before it can be transferred to storage.

Cooling water is circulated through the jacket at a high enough flow rate that the jacket temperature stays essentially constant at 15 $^\circ$C throughout. The rate of heat transfer from the batch to the jacket is *not* constant — it depends on the temperature difference between the batch and the jacket:

$$\dot{Q} = UA\,(T_{jacket} - T)$$

where $T$ is the (uniform) batch temperature and $UA$ is the overall heat transfer coefficient multiplied by the heat transfer area.

The vessel is agitated by a mechanical stirrer which draws a constant 5.0 kW, all of which is dissipated into the liquid.

The following data are provided:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass of batch | 500 kg |
| Batch heat capacity ($C_P$) | 3.2 kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ |
| Initial batch temperature | 90 $^\circ$C |
| Target batch temperature | 30 $^\circ$C |
| Jacket temperature | 15 $^\circ$C |
| $UA$ | 1200 W K$^{-1}$ |
| Stirrer power | 5.0 kW |

**(a)** Starting from the general energy balance, derive the differential equation describing the batch temperature as a function of time. State and justify every assumption you use. For this part only, assume the stirrer is switched off.

**(b)** Separate the variables and integrate to obtain an expression for $T(t)$. 

**(c)** Calculate the time required to cool the batch from 90 $^\circ$C to 30 $^\circ$C with the stirrer off.

**(d)** Repeat the derivation with the stirrer running. Show that the batch now approaches a steady-state temperature $T_\infty$ rather than the jacket temperature, and calculate $T_\infty$.

**(e)** Calculate the time required to reach 30 $^\circ$C with the stirrer running, and comment on the difference from part (c).

**(f)** A colleague proposes reaching 18 $^\circ$C by simply leaving the vessel cooling for longer with the stirrer running. Explain why this will not work, and suggest two changes that would.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**(a) Differential equation (stirrer off)**

Assumptions:

- Batch (closed) system — nothing enters or leaves $\Rightarrow \dot{m}_{in} = \dot{m}_{out} = 0$.
- Well-mixed vessel $\Rightarrow$ a single uniform temperature $T$ describes the whole batch at any instant. Without this we could not write a single $T$ at all.
- No shaft work with the stirrer off $\Rightarrow \dot{W} = 0$.
- The mass of the batch $m$ and its heat capacity $C_P$ are constant.
- The jacket temperature $T_{jacket}$ and $UA$ are constant.

Starting from the general energy balance:

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

With no flow and no work:

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \dot{Q}$$

Since the batch mass is constant it comes outside the derivative, and for a liquid with constant $C_P$ and no phase change or reaction, $dH_{sys} = C_P\,dT$:

$$m\,C_P\,\frac{dT}{dt} = \dot{Q} = UA\,(T_{jacket} - T)$$

This is the key difference from a constant-duty problem: the driving force shrinks as the batch cools, so $\dot{Q}$ is a function of the very variable we are solving for.

**(b) Integration**

Separate the variables:

$$\frac{dT}{T - T_{jacket}} = -\frac{UA}{m\,C_P}\,dt$$

Integrate from $T_0$ at $t=0$ to $T$ at time $t$:

$$\int_{T_0}^{T}\frac{dT}{T - T_{jacket}} = -\frac{UA}{m\,C_P}\int_0^t dt$$

$$\ln\!\left(\frac{T - T_{jacket}}{T_0 - T_{jacket}}\right) = -\frac{UA}{m\,C_P}\,t$$

$$T(t) = T_{jacket} + (T_0 - T_{jacket})\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{UA}{m\,C_P}\,t\right)$$

The temperature approaches the jacket temperature exponentially rather than linearly. 

**(c) Cooling time, stirrer off**

Rearranging for $t$:

$$t = \left(\frac{mC_P}{UA}\right) \ln\!\left(\frac{T_0 - T_{jacket}}{T - T_{jacket}}\right)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
t & = 1333 \times \ln\!\left(\frac{90 - 15}{30 - 15}\right) \\
  & = 1333 \times \ln(5.00) \\
  & = 1333 \times 1.609 \\
  & = 2146\ \text{s} = 35.8\ \text{min}
\end{aligned}
$$

**(d) With the stirrer running**

The stirrer adds work to the system, so $\dot{W} = +5.0$ kW (energy transferred *into* the system, consistent with the sign convention):

$$m\,C_P\,\frac{dT}{dt} = UA\,(T_{jacket} - T) + \dot{W}$$

At steady state the left-hand side is zero, so the batch stops cooling when the heat removed equals the work added:

$$0 = UA\,(T_{jacket} - T_\infty) + \dot{W} \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_\infty = T_{jacket} + \frac{\dot{W}}{UA}$$

$$T_\infty = 15 + \frac{5000}{1200} = 15 + 4.17 = 19.2\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

The batch can never reach the jacket temperature while the stirrer runs — the stirrer is a continuous heat source of 5 kW.

Rewriting the differential equation in terms of $T_\infty$ shows the mathematics is unchanged:

$$m\,C_P\,\frac{dT}{dt} = UA\,(T_\infty - T)$$

$$T(t) = T_\infty + (T_0 - T_\infty)\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{UA}{m\,C_P}\,t\right)$$

**(e) Cooling time with the stirrer running**

$$
\begin{aligned}
t & = \frac{mC_P}{UA}\,\ln\!\left(\frac{T_0 - T_\infty}{T - T_\infty}\right) \\
  & = 1333 \times \ln\!\left(\frac{90 - 19.2}{30 - 19.2}\right) \\
  & = 1333 \times \ln(6.56) \\
  & = 1333 \times 1.881 \\
  & = 2507\ \text{s} = 41.8\ \text{min}
\end{aligned}
$$

The stirrer adds about 6 minutes (17%) to the cooling time. The 5 kW of stirrer power is small compared with the initial cooling duty ($UA \times 75 = 90$ kW), so it barely matters at the start — but it becomes an ever-larger fraction of the duty as the driving force shrinks, which is why it disproportionately affects the tail of the curve.

**(f) Why 18 $^\circ$C is not reachable**

The batch asymptotes to $T_\infty = 19.2$ $^\circ$C, so 18 $^\circ$C is impossible no matter how long the vessel is left — the exponential approaches the asymptote but never crosses it. "Leave it longer" fails because the limit is set by an energy balance, not by time.

Two changes that would work:

1. **Lower the jacket temperature** — use chilled water instead of cooling water. Dropping $T_{jacket}$ to 5 $^\circ$C moves $T_\infty$ to $5 + 4.17 = 9.2$ $^\circ$C, putting 18 $^\circ$C comfortably in range and reaching it far faster.
2. **Increase $UA$**, or reduce the stirrer power once the batch is homogeneous. Doubling $UA$ to 2400 W/K halves both the time constant and the stirrer's temperature penalty ($T_\infty = 15 + 2.1 = 17.1$ $^\circ$C). Reducing the agitation to 1 kW gives $T_\infty = 15.8$ $^\circ$C, though it risks losing the well-mixed assumption the whole analysis depends on.
